introduction-the-traffic-cop.core: A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of servers so no single server is overwhelmed, and it removes failed servers from rotation. That gives horizontal scaling, high availability and zero-downtime deploys (drain, update, re-add). The design choices are which layer it works at (L4 vs L7), which algorithm, how it checks health, and how packets flow back (proxy vs DSR).

first_principles.problem: A single web server hits 100% CPU during peak while the company's two spare servers sit idle.
truths: Clients need a single stable entry point.
derivation: Put a **VIP** in front of a pool.

analogy.title: A traffic officer at a busy junction
analogy.story: Directs cars to the least busy lanes and closes lanes with accidents.
analogy.breaks: Officers see congestion visually; LBs rely on metrics and health checks.

check.q: How does a load balancer enable zero-downtime deploys?
check.a: By draining a server (no new requests, finishing existing ones), updating it, and re-adding it while others serve traffic.

layer-4-l4-balancing-the-packet-shovel.core: An L4 balancer decides per connection using IPs and ports, without reading the payload. It's fast (millions of packets per second, often in-kernel or hardware), protocol-agnostic (TCP, UDP, TLS passthrough) and keeps the backend connection 1:1 with the client's. It can't route by URL or header, can't see HTTP errors, and balances connections rather than requests.

first_principles.problem: A team needs to balance raw TCP database and MQTT traffic at very high throughput.
truths: Headers up to L4 are enough to pick a backend.

analogy.title: A mail sorter reading only postcodes
analogy.story: Very fast because it never opens envelopes, but it can't route by what's written inside.
analogy.breaks: Mail is one-off; connections persist and pin load.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: In-kernel TCP balancing at line rate.

code.text:
ipvsadm -A -t 10.0.0.100:5432 -s lc           # least-connections
ipvsadm -a -t 10.0.0.100:5432 -r 10.0.1.21:5432 -m
ipvsadm -a -t 10.0.0.100:5432 -r 10.0.1.22:5432 -m
ipvsadm -Ln --stats

check.q: Why does L4 balancing struggle with HTTP/2 or gRPC?
check.a: All requests share long-lived connections, so balancing per connection pins many requests to one backend.

layer-7-l7-balancing-the-application-pro.core: An L7 balancer terminates the client connection, parses HTTP (or gRPC), and opens its own connections to backends. It can route by host, path, header or cookie, balance per request, retry idempotent requests, add headers, terminate TLS, compress, cache and observe status codes. The cost is CPU, a bit of latency and running a full proxy. Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy and AWS ALB are typical.

first_principles.problem: /api must go to API servers, /static to object storage, and gRPC calls must spread per request.
truths: Requests are the true unit of work.

analogy.title: A receptionist who reads each request
analogy.story: They read why you're visiting and send you to the right department and the least busy person.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists are slow; proxies add only milliseconds, but do cost CPU.

check.q: Name two things an L7 LB can do that an L4 LB cannot.
check.a: Route by URL path/host/header and balance per HTTP request (also retries on 5xx, header rewriting).

balancing-algorithms-round-robin-weighte.core: Round robin cycles through servers, which is simple and fair when requests and servers are similar. Weighted round robin sends proportionally more to bigger servers. Least connections picks the server with the fewest active connections, adapting to uneven request durations. Power-of-two-choices (pick two at random and send to the less loaded) gets near-optimal balance with little coordination, which suits many LB instances.

first_principles.problem: Round robin overloads one server because some requests take 10 s while most take 10 ms.
truths: Global state is expensive across many LBs.

analogy.title: Supermarket checkouts
analogy.story: Taking turns works when baskets are similar; with a few full trolleys, pick the shortest queue.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers see queues; LBs see only their own counts unless shared.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Big server gets more; long requests don't pile up.

code.text:
backend app
  balance leastconn
  server a 10.0.1.11:8080 weight 100 check slowstart 30s
  server b 10.0.1.12:8080 weight 100 check slowstart 30s
  server c 10.0.1.13:8080 weight 200 check slowstart 30s   # 2× bigger

check.q: Why is power-of-two-choices popular in large distributed LBs?
check.a: It achieves near-least-loaded balance using only two random samples, without global coordination between LB instances.

algorithm-consistent-hashing-and-the-thu.core: Hash-based balancing maps a key (client IP, session ID, cache key) to a backend, giving stickiness and better cache locality. Plain modulo hashing remaps almost everything when the pool changes, sending a thundering herd of cache misses to backends. Consistent hashing (ring or Maglev) remaps only about 1/N of keys. Bounded-load variants cap any backend's share to avoid hot spots.

first_principles.problem: Scaling a cache tier from 8 to 9 nodes behind a modulo-hash LB causes a 90% miss storm that overloads the database.
truths: Hot keys can overload one backend.

analogy.title: Assigned seating that survives a new table
analogy.story: Adding a table only moves the few guests nearest it, not everyone.
analogy.breaks: Guests move politely; cache misses hit the database all at once.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Adding a node remaps ~11% of keys, not ~89%.

code.text:
clusters:
  - name: cache
    lb_policy: RING_HASH
    ring_hash_lb_config: { minimum_ring_size: 1024 }
# route: hash_policy: [{ header: { header_name: "x-cache-key" } }]

check.q: What's the 'thundering herd' in hash-based load balancing?
check.a: When a pool change remaps most keys, caches miss en masse and the flood of requests overwhelms backends.

health-checks-how-the-lb-knows-a-server-.core: Active health checks probe each backend periodically (TCP connect, HTTP GET /healthz expecting 200) and mark it down after N failures and up after M successes. Passive checks (outlier detection) watch real traffic for errors or timeouts. Good health endpoints test what matters (can serve requests) without cascading: a /healthz that checks a shared database can eject every server at once during a DB blip.

first_principles.problem: A DB hiccup makes every server's /healthz fail, so the LB ejects them all and the site goes fully down.
truths: Failed servers must be removed fast.
derivation: Avoid **deep dependency checks** in LB health.

analogy.title: A supervisor checking staff are at their posts
analogy.story: They check regularly, but don't send everyone home just because the shared coffee machine broke.
analogy.breaks: Supervisors judge context; checks follow fixed rules.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bad servers ejected; never more than half the pool.

code.text:
health_checks:
  - timeout: 1s
    interval: 5s
    unhealthy_threshold: 3
    healthy_threshold: 2
    http_health_check: { path: /ready }
outlier_detection:
  consecutive_5xx: 5
  base_ejection_time: 30s
  max_ejection_percent: 50

check.q: Why limit max_ejection_percent in outlier detection?
check.a: To prevent a widespread or correlated issue from ejecting so many backends that the remaining ones collapse.

direct-server-return-dsr-the-asymmetric-.core: Responses are usually much larger than requests. With Direct Server Return, the LB forwards only inbound packets (rewriting the MAC or encapsulating them), and backends reply straight to the client using the VIP as source, bypassing the LB on the way out. That gives huge outbound throughput with small LBs. The cost is that backends must hold the VIP on loopback (with ARP suppressed), there is no L7 processing, and asymmetric paths complicate firewalls and debugging.

first_principles.problem: A video service's LBs saturate at 40 Gbps outbound while inbound requests are only 400 Mbps.
truths: LBs only need to pick the backend.
Return path can skip the LB.

analogy.title: A receptionist who routes visitors, and visitors leave by the back door
analogy.story: The front desk handles arrivals only; departures don't crowd it.
analogy.breaks: Buildings have one address; backends must pretend to own the VIP.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: LB handles 400 Mbps in; backends send 40 Gbps out directly.

code.text:
# LB
ipvsadm -A -t 203.0.113.10:80 -s mh
ipvsadm -a -t 203.0.113.10:80 -r 10.0.1.21 -g     # -g = gatewaying (DSR)
# each backend
ip addr add 203.0.113.10/32 dev lo
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore=1 net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_announce=2

check.q: Why must backends suppress ARP for the VIP in DSR?
check.a: Otherwise they'd answer ARP for the VIP and steal inbound traffic from the LB on the shared network.
